source: Scientists look closely, use their senses and tools, and ask questions they can test. An observation is what you notice; a guess about why is a hypothesis.
Children mix up what they saw with what they think caused it. "The ice melted" is an observation; "the sun melted it" is a guess to test.
Science starts with noticing. A scientist looks closely, listens, smells and feels (but never tastes anything in a lab), and writes down what she finds. Then she asks a question she could test.
An observation is something you notice with your senses or a tool: "The puddle got smaller by noon." A hypothesis is a guess about why that you can test: "The sun dried the puddle."
Tools help your senses: a hand lens sees small things, a ruler measures, a thermometer reads temperature, a balance compares mass and a timer counts seconds. The notebook remembers.
Good questions can be tested. "Why are flowers pretty?" is hard to test. "Do bean seeds sprout faster in a warm room or a cool room?" can be tested with seeds, two rooms and a calendar.
Mia writes: "The ice cube on the plate melted in 20 minutes. I think the warm air melted it."
The first sentence is an observation; the second is a hypothesis.
"The ice cube melted in 20 minutes" is what she saw and timed: an observation.
"I think the warm air melted it" is her idea about why: a hypothesis she could test.
Writing a guess as if you saw it. "The dog was hungry" is a guess; "the dog ate all its food in one minute" is what you observed.
Going further. The Handbook of Nature-Study is full of things to observe outdoors, and the Science Lab lets you test ideas on screen.
